sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Grant County, KY?
sections.html:
Three Williamstown-area offices touch a Grant County tax bill. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets the value, the Grant County Sheriff collects the current-year bill, and the Grant County Clerk takes over once a bill goes delinquent. None of them sets the rate. Each taxing district, such as the county, a school system or a city, decides its own levy.

The PVA works from the courthouse at 101 North Main Street in Williamstown and answers at (859) 824-6511. The Sheriff's Office is at 212 Barnes Road, Suite A, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and its office line is (859) 824-3333. Payments can also be mailed to PO Box 235, Dry Ridge, KY 41035. For delinquent bills, the county directory points to the Clerk at (859) 824-3321.

The sheriff does not collect any city taxes. Williamstown, Dry Ridge, Corinth and Crittenden each handle their own, so call city hall if a line on your closing statement looks like a municipal charge.

sections.h2: When are Grant County property tax bills due, and what do late bills cost?
sections.html:
Bills are mailed and viewable online on October 1, and the sheriff accepts payment from that day through April 15. The cheapest window is October 1 to November 1, when a 2 percent discount applies. Partial payments are refused, so the full bill has to be paid at once.

Grant County Sheriff's listed collection schedule (source: Grant County Sheriff's Office, property tax page)
DatesWhat applies
October 1 to November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Face value
January 1 to January 315 percent penalty
February 1 to April 1521 percent penalty, as the sheriff lists it
After April 15Bill moves to the County Clerk

KRS 134.015 sets the 2 percent discount and the 5 percent January penalty. The statute's later penalty is 10 percent, which is lower than the 21 percent the sheriff lists for February through April 15. Ask the sheriff's office for a written payoff before you sign anything.

The sheriff pays by cash, check, debit or credit card, and the card company adds a small fee. Mailed payments get a receipt back only if you include a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

sections.h2: Why did the tax bill come in the previous owner's name?
sections.html:
Kentucky bills the person who owned the parcel on January 1. A buyer who closes in March or August will usually see that year's bill addressed to the seller, because the sheriff does not receive new deed transfers. The seller is expected to forward it.

  • Put the proration of that year's bill in the contract, since the county will not split it for you.
  • Have the deed list the buyer's in-care-of address, which KRS 382.135 requires so later bills reach the right mailbox.
  • Ask the PVA to confirm the mailing address on record after the deed is recorded.

In a quick as-is sale, the title company usually pays the open year's bill from the seller's proceeds, but the contract should say so in plain words.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Grant County assessment?
sections.html:
Begin with a conference at the PVA's office, because Kentucky does not let you file an appeal without one. Assessment notices go out first, and the tax roll then opens for public inspection for 13 days starting the first Monday in May.

  • Meet with the PVA or a deputy, who must explain how the value was reached and write up the conference.
  • File the appeal with the County Clerk by the close of business on the day after inspection ends.
  • Bring evidence such as sales of similar houses, repair estimates, insurance records or construction costs. Without documents the local board denies the appeal.
  • Attend the hearing, set 25 to 35 days after inspection ends. Missing it ends your right to go on to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

If bills are printed before the board rules, your own opinion of value is used. A higher final value produces a supplemental bill for the difference.

sections.h2: Is there a homestead exemption in Grant County?
sections.html:
Yes, for owners who are 65 or older or classified as totally disabled. For the 2025 and 2026 assessment years the state exemption is $49,100, taken off the assessed value before tax is figured. On a Grant County house assessed at $250,000, the taxable figure drops to $200,900.

Applications go to the Grant County PVA, which also handles disability claims. Proof of age can be a birth certificate, driver's license or passport. Disability filers who are not veterans with a service-connected rating, or ruled permanently disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems, have to reapply every year.

The sheriff's office does not process exemptions and sends callers straight to the PVA. If you sell, tell the PVA so the exemption comes off the old address.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Grant County taxes when I sell?
sections.html:
The debt follows the parcel. The sheriff deals only with current-year taxes. After the April 15 transfer, the Grant County Clerk holds the bill and a lien is recorded. Under KRS 134.015 that lien lasts until it is paid or the 11-year period in KRS 134.420 ends, whoever owns the house.

The state's own example shows how fast a delinquent bill grows. A $1,000 bill becomes a $1,254 certificate of delinquency at transfer after a 10 percent penalty, a sheriff's fee and the sheriff's commission. Then 1 percent interest accrues each month, the clerk adds 10 percent, and the county attorney adds 20 percent once the first notice goes out. A $10 fee covers recording and releasing the lien.

A tax sale can follow 90 to 135 days after transfer, and a third-party buyer who purchases the certificate may add charges. Anyone selling a Grant County house with back taxes should get a payoff from the Clerk before listing. A cash sale can clear the lien at closing, with the balance deducted from the price.

sections.h2: What should a Grant County seller know about the county itself?
sections.html:
Grant County sits in northern Kentucky and belongs to the Cincinnati metropolitan area. It was formed in 1820 from Pendleton County and covers 258 square miles of land. Williamstown is the county seat, and Dry Ridge, Corinth and Crittenden are the other incorporated cities. Students attend Grant County Schools or Williamstown Independent Schools, and the Ark Encounter in Williamstown draws visitors from across the region.

Census QuickFacts gives this picture of the county:

  • Population: 26,181 in 2025, up 5.0 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $209,500, with 75.1 percent of homes owner-occupied.
  • Median household income: $69,178, and a mean commute of 26.9 minutes.
  • Median gross rent: $862, and 110 building permits issued in 2025.

A house with deferred repairs or a tax lien can sell more cleanly to a buyer who pays cash and closes as-is.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Grant County, KY?
faqs.a: The Grant County Sheriff's Office collects current-year bills at 212 Barnes Road, Suite A in Williamstown, phone (859) 824-3333. The Grant County Clerk handles bills that went delinquent after April 15.

faqs.q: What is the last day to get the discount on a Grant County tax bill?
faqs.a: November 1. The sheriff gives a 2 percent discount from October 1 through that date, face value from November 2 to December 31, and penalties from January 1.

faqs.q: Can I pay half of my Grant County property tax bill now and half later?
faqs.a: No. The sheriff states that the bill must be paid in full and does not accept partial payments. Plan for the whole amount when you choose which payment window to use.

faqs.q: How much is the Kentucky homestead exemption for a Grant County home?
faqs.a: It is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. You must be 65 or older, or totally disabled, and you apply through the Grant County PVA at (859) 824-6511.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay Grant County back taxes before selling my house?
faqs.a: Not before listing, but the lien stays with the property, so the balance gets paid at closing. Ask the Grant County Clerk for a payoff figure first so the title company can plan for it.
